interviewQuestions.question: How would you structure the frontend codebase for a product with 15 teams shipping features in parallel?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from feature-based structure rather than type-based folders: each team owns a `features/<name>/` directory containing its own components, hooks, and tests, so a team's changes stay physically isolated and deleting a feature is deleting one folder. Cross-cutting code splits into two layers above that — a design system for shared UI primitives, and a thin set of app-shell/routing code that composes features together.

The rule I'd enforce is dependency direction: app shell can depend on features and the design system; features can depend on the design system; the design system depends on nothing feature-specific. I'd back this with lint rules (e.g. an import boundary linter) rather than trusting convention, because with 15 teams someone will eventually import across a feature boundary by accident.

Ownership matters as much as folder layout — I'd want `CODEOWNERS` mapping each feature folder to its team and a dedicated platform team owning the design system and shared tooling, so 'shared code' has an actual owner and doesn't rot into an unmaintained dumping ground.

**Testing:** whether you reach for structural boundaries and enforcement (lint, ownership), not just a folder-naming preference.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Your design system's `Button` component has accumulated 12 boolean props over two years, mostly used by a single consumer each. How do you fix this without breaking every existing usage?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't rip it out in one release — that breaks every consumer at once and burns trust in the design system. I'd introduce the better API alongside the old one: add a `variant` prop and slot-based composition, mark the old booleans `@deprecated` in types and docs, and keep both working for a release window.

Concretely: ship the new API in a minor release (additive, non-breaking), write a codemod that mechanically rewrites the common boolean combinations to the new variant prop, and give teams a deprecation window — a console warning when a deprecated prop is used, removed only in the next major version after teams have had time to run the codemod. I'd track adoption with a lint rule that flags any new usage of the deprecated props, so the count only shrinks from here.

The part people skip is measuring before acting: I'd grep actual usage first to see which boolean combinations are real versus dead code, since some of those 12 props may have zero live consumers and can just be deleted outright.

**Testing:** whether you can plan a non-breaking migration for a widely-consumed component, or would default to a disruptive rewrite.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Migration

interviewQuestions.question: Would you recommend a monorepo or polyrepo for a company with three product teams sharing one design system?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd lean monorepo at this scale, with a caveat about tooling. Three teams sharing one design system is exactly the case a monorepo optimizes for: a breaking change to a shared component shows up in the same CI run as every consumer, so it's caught before merge instead of discovered by a downstream team weeks later after an independent publish.

The caveat is that a monorepo without incremental build tooling degrades badly as it grows — if every CI run rebuilds and retests all three apps for every change, that cost compounds. So I'd pair the monorepo decision with an affected-only build tool (Nx or Turborepo) from day one, not bolted on after CI hits 20+ minutes.

I'd flip the recommendation toward polyrepo only if the three teams' release cadences and tooling genuinely diverge — say, one team is on a different framework version entirely — because then the monorepo's atomic-change benefit is smaller than the friction of forcing shared CI config and lint rules on teams that don't want them.

**Testing:** whether you can match the repo strategy to the actual coupling between teams, not apply one as a default.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A design system change that looked backward-compatible broke three consuming apps in production. How do you debug why, and what process gap does it point to?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First I'd isolate which specific change broke each app — a prop's default value, a CSS class rename, or a behavior change (like a modal now trapping focus) are the usual suspects for a change that looked additive but wasn't. 'Backward compatible' often only means 'the types still compile,' which misses runtime and visual regressions entirely.

That gap is the real finding: the release process was missing a check that would have caught this before publish — most commonly, no automated visual-regression suite (pixel-diffing every component's stories against the previous version) and no canary/beta release consumed by one internal app before the general release. I'd propose adding both: visual regression as a CI gate on the design-system repo, and a pre-release channel that at least one real consumer's staging environment pulls from before a version goes to everyone.

I'd also check whether semver was actually followed — if this was published as a patch or minor but changed visible behavior, that's a process violation independent of the technical cause, and worth calling out explicitly so it doesn't repeat.

**Testing:** whether you can trace a production incident back to a missing process control, not just the line of code that changed.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging
